Asymptotic size in Marmara chub Squalius cii, a freshwater cyprinid endemic to the Marmara region of Turkey, was estimated through photographic analysis of large adult specimens collected during spring surveys. The ultimate fork length, corresponding to the theoretical maximum body size, was calculated to be 27.5 cm [Li = 27.5 cm] using a conversion factor applied to the measured total length, which reached 28.9 cm in the largest recorded individual. This value positions the species as a medium-sized member within the genus, comparable in maximum dimensions to certain populations of the related roach Rutilus rutilus. Growth trajectories derived from length-frequency data suggest that asymptotic size is approached gradually, with most somatic expansion occurring during the first few years of life. The acquisition of such large body size is likely constrained by the seasonal productivity and thermal regime of the lentic and slow-flowing habitats this species occupies, where resource availability can fluctuate markedly between summer and winter months. Males and females do not appear to differ substantially in ultimate length, although sample sizes remain limited for very large size classes beyond 25 cm.

Reproductive development in Squalius cii involves the onset of maturity at a relatively modest body length. The fork length at which 50 percent of individuals attain puberty is estimated at 7.6 cm [Lp = 7.6 cm], a value inferred through allometric comparison with the well-studied congener Rutilus rutilus, for which detailed maturity ogives exist. This size threshold corresponds roughly to the transition from the juvenile growth phase to the period of active gonadal recrudescence. Individuals below this fork length typically display no macroscopic evidence of gonad development, while those exceeding it rapidly initiate gametogenesis as the spawning season approaches. The relatively small size at puberty suggests that Squalius cii adopts an early-maturing life-history strategy, potentially allowing it to compensate for elevated natural mortality rates by reproducing at a younger age than would be expected for a cyprinid of its ultimate body size. This pattern aligns with the life-history profiles of other Mediterranean freshwater fishes exposed to unpredictable hydrological conditions.

The gonadosomatic index (GSI) reaches an average peak value of 5% [GSI = 5%] in gravid individuals sampled during the prespawning period at a water temperature of 22 °C [T = 22 °C]. This assessment was conducted at a water temperature of 22 °C [T = 22 °C], conditions representative of late spring in the species' native lowland streams and lake margins. The high relative ovary mass indicates substantial allocation of somatic reserves toward egg production, a common feature among batch-spawning cyprinids that produce multiple clutches within a single reproductive season. The observed index is consistent with values reported for other Squalius species from similar latitudes, although interannual variation linked to food availability and thermal conditions can shift the prespawning peak by up to 15 percent. Histological examination of ovarian tissue at this stage confirms the presence of oocytes in advanced vitellogenic stages.

Egg size in this species was estimated using a comparative approach based on the well-documented oocyte diameter of another leuciscid, Rutilus rutilus, which produces eggs approximately 2.0 mm in diameter. Applying this diameter to a spherical egg model yields a wet weight at birth of approximately 0.0042 grams [Wwb = approximately 0.0042 grams], a value that falls within the typical range for cyprinids of comparable adult size. This relatively small mass at the onset of exogenous feeding reflects an altricial life-history mode in which newly hatched larvae rely on endogenous yolk reserves for a brief period before transitioning to active foraging. The small body size at this developmental stage imposes constraints on initial prey selection, limiting newly emerged larvae to microscopic zooplankton such as rotifers and copepod nauplii. Larval survival during this critical window is heavily influenced by the temporal match between hatching and peak plankton abundance, which in turn depends on the thermal regime of the spawning habitat during early spring.

Maximum longevity in Squalius cii is estimated at approximately 14 years [am = approximately 14 years] based on extrapolation from mark-recapture studies and scale-reading analyses of the closely related roach Rutilus rutilus, which exhibits comparable life-history characteristics under similar thermal conditions at a temperature of 22 °C [T = 22 °C]. This lifespan estimate applies to populations experiencing a mean annual water temperature of 22 °C [T = 22 °C], a value consistent with the warm lowland waters this species inhabits during the active growing season. The attainment of such an extended lifespan is notable for a fish of modest body size and suggests a relatively slow pace of senescence, possibly linked to a low intrinsic metabolic rate and the absence of intense predation pressure in certain refuge habitats. Old individuals, exceeding 12 years of age, are rarely captured in standard survey gear, implying either elevated natural mortality in the oldest age classes or a behavioral shift that reduces catchability. Long-term demographic studies would be valuable to confirm whether age-related reproductive senescence occurs in the oldest females.
